newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Ex-communist bosses still in majority in ex-USSR.
newsitem.headline: Ex-communist bosses still in majority in ex-USSR.

text.p: The victory of a former communist candidate seeking closer ties with Russia highlights the continuity between old and new political elites in most countries of the former Soviet Union.
Of the 15 union republics which made up the USSR, only the three fiercely independent Baltic States are outside the Commonwealth of Independent States, founded at the end of 1991.
Here, five years after the Soviet Union collapsed, is an outline of their political and economic systems and leaders.

MOLDOVA - Parliamentary speaker Petru Lucinschi, a former communist who now describes himself as a social democrat, defeated incumbent Mircea Snegur, also a former top party official, in Sunday's second round of the presidential election.

He attacked Snegur's economic record during the campaign and played on concern from Moldova's large Russian-speaking minority about Snegur's call for closer ties to Romania, from whose land and people Josef Stalin carved most of Moldova in 1940.

RUSSIA - Boris Yeltsin, a communist turned market reformer, won a second term in office on July 3 but immediately disappeared from public view with heart problems and underwent a bypass operation on November 5.

His government, led by former gas industry chief Viktor Chernomyurdin, has vowed to press on with reforms, but he faces tough opposition from a parliament dominated by communists and other conservatives. The constitution gives the president strong powers and parliament is relatively weak.
UKRAINE - Leonid Kuchma, once manager of the world's largest missile plant, was elected Ukraine's second president in July 1994, but communists and nationalists dominate the parliament.
The constitution gives Kuchma strong powers and he has moved steadily to create a market economy in the country, which was the breadbasket of the Soviet Union.
BELARUS - President Alexander Lukashenko won sweeping powers in a referendum last month and has since replaced the old communist-dominated parliament with a more compliant body.
Lukashenko, criticised for human rights violations, especially a crackdown on independent media, has slowed down market reforms. The International Monetary Fund has pulled out.
LATVIA - Non-executive president Guntis Ulmanis is elected by parliament and there is a coalition government, spanning the political spectrum from nationalists to left-of-centre.
The coalition, nearly one year old, is led by a businessman, Andris Shkele, a strong proponent of EU and NATO membership.
ESTONIA - Prime Minister Tiit Vaehi runs a minority government of 40 MPs in the 101-seat parliament after his former coalition partners walked out.
He favours integration with the West and continuing the market reforms which have made the smallest of the Baltic states a leader in economic reform.

LITHUANIA - The right-wing Homeland Union of Vytautas Landsbergis, who spearheaded the drive to independence five years ago, won parliamentary elections by a landslide last month and has formed a coalition with the Christian Democrats.
The head of state is President Algirdas Brazauskas, a communist who defied the Soviet authorities and whose actions played a major part in the implosion of the superpower.

ARMENIA - Soviet-era dissident Levon Ter-Petrosyan was re-elected for a second term in office in September in an election marred by opposition allegations of vote-rigging and unfair practices. The constitutional court, dominated by Ter-Petrosyan appointees, upheld the vote last month.
Parliament is also dominated by the president's supporters and Prime Minister Armen Sarkisyan has vowed to step up market reforms in the impoverished Transcaucasian country.

AZERBAIJAN - The oil-rich Transcaucasus country is ruled with an iron fist by former Soviet politburo member Haidar Aliyev, a favourite of one-time Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev Aliyev won extra powers in a referendum in November 1995.
Aliyev's centrist party controls parliament.

GEORGIA - Eduard Shevardnadze, a former leader of the Georgian Communist Party who then became the last foreign minister of the Soviet Union, brought his country reluctantly into the CIS, a loose grouping which succeeded the superpower.

His main worry is a separatist drive from Ossetians in the north, who want to merge with ethnic kin across the border in Russia and Abkhazians on the Black Sea coast, who held their own vote for a local parliament last month.

KAZAKHSTAN - The energy-rich state is the the second largest CIS country in size after Russia and is ruled by Communist-era boss Nursultan Nazarbayev, who has won strong executive presidential powers. The next election is due in 2000.
Foreign investors are bullish but economic hardships, tensions between Kazakhs and Russians and Russia's grip on the republic's oil expert routes make for an uncertain future.
KYRGYZSTAN - The mountainous republic of 4.5 million is led by former physicist Askar Akayev. Once hailed as a democrat, he has increased executive powers at parliament's expense.
The economy is stabilising, but it remains heavily dependent on agriculture and gold. Ethnic tensions in the fertile Osh Valley in the south have also caused concern.

TAJIKISTAN - A four-year civil war has killed tens of thousands and displaced many more. President Imomali Rakhmonov's shaky administration is threatened by Islamic insurgency and seething clan rivalries.

The IMF said the economy had begun to stabilise, but there has been no substantial economic development since independence in 1991. Tajikistan remains more dependent on Russia for military and economic support than any of the other former Soviet states.
TURKMENISTAN - The energy-rich nation is ruled by former Communist Party functionary Saparmurat Niyazov who tolerates no opposition and has fostered a Stalin-style personality cult.
Niyazov is keen to develop Turmkenistan's huge gas reserves to turn the economy around, but patience is wearing thin.
UZBEKISTAN - Led by tough-talking president and former Communist Party boss Islam Karimov, Uzbekistan aims to be political leader in the Central Asian region.

But Karimov's ambiguous commitment to market reform has worried foreign investors while the government's approach to human rights and intolerance of opposition has got in the way of Karimov's ambition for close relations with the United States.
